label: reading_error_messages
graph_version: 3.9.8 (3.9.7 + one primary per misconception (S9c) and the four remaining sibling edges (S9b), 2026-11-04; listed in revision_3_9_8)

edges.label:
[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday reading: an error message is like a teacher's correction, naming the exact mistake, its line and its fix, one message per mistake. Java rule: the message reports what javac detected and where it noticed it; one fault can cause several messages and the suggested remedy may be wrong.
[1] misconception (M) -> ErrorLineIsFaultLine: wrong rule: The line number in a javac error is always the line that has the mistake. Right rule: The compiler reports where it noticed the problem, which can be after the real fault.
[2] misconception (M) -> FixEveryErrorMessage: wrong rule: Each error message is a separate mistake that needs its own fix. Right rule: One fault can produce several messages; fix the first and recompile.
[3] misconception (M) -> CompilerSuggestionIsFix: wrong rule: Doing exactly what the compiler message suggests will fix the error. Right rule: An error message is evidence that something is wrong, but its suggested remedy may be wrong; find the actual cause.
[4] inconsistent_trace (T) -> ErrorLineIsFaultLine: Applies the read-first-error rule unevenly: starts from the first message on one compile but from the last on another, or looks only at the reported line without checking the lines before it. (here mixing in: "The line number in a javac error is always the line that has the mistake")

[0] names_the_element (N): Reading error messages is the debugging skill of interpreting a compiler (or JVM) message, File.java:line: description, to locate and fix the fault.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Each javac message gives the file, the line where the error was detected and a description; only the first message is truly reliable, and the real error is generally at or before the reported line.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Read the first message, go to its line, look there and then backwards for the cause, fix that one error, recompile, and repeat.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Reading 'Bad.java:2: '{' expected' yields the location (file Bad.java, line 2) and the kind of problem (a missing left brace); with a later or vaguer message, it yields only where to start looking.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One read-fix-recompile cycle removes one fault and often several messages; the message count after recompiling can drop sharply.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Compile-time errors are found and fixed by reading their messages; the message maps imperfectly to the fault.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Reading an error message tells you where to start looking; debugging goes on from there to the cause.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Purpose: use the compiler as a friend that says something is wrong, turning its message into a hypothesis about the fault.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> ErrorLineIsFaultLine: Introducing a known mistake into a working program and reading the resulting message shows which messages a fault produces; adding a fault earlier in the file can change messages reported later.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Read messages first-error-first whenever javac or the JVM reports an error; for logic errors there is no message, so use tracing and print statements instead.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Reported line = where javac noticed the problem. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: a missing brace or quote, reported lines later (e.g. reached end of file while parsing)
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Suggested remedies are unreliable. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: a message whose literal advice (e.g. declare a class abstract) is wrong
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Run-time messages name the exception and the line. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: reading Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: 0 at UseArgument.main(UseArgument.java:6)
